Rev 3.2 — 4S3P, a common-port BMS, and USB-C charging

The pack is 12 cells in 4 rows of 3, not the 36 the record claimed. That one fact overturns the diagnosis: the 4S board already fitted is the correct part, the pack really was flat, and the fix is a charger — not a new BMS.

Rev3.1 Supersedes3.0 — assumed 3S Date2026-08-11 Pack4S3P · ~130 Wh ERC0 violations

00 What changed, and why it matters

The BMS was never the fault A 4S BMS on a 4S pack is the right part doing its job. At the measured 12.22 V a 4S pack sits at 3.05 V per cell — genuinely low — and a group dragged under the cutoff latches it off. The ~0.55 V across B− to P− was correct behaviour, not a defect. Do not fit the 3S board. Charge the pack instead.
The same evidence, read two ways
ObservationRead as 3S (wrong)Read as 4S (correct)
12.22 V pack 4.07 V/cell — nearly full, so a BMS refusing to conduct must be faulty 3.05 V/cell — genuinely low. One weak group easily sits under the under-voltage cutoff
B−→P− ≈ 0.55 V body diodes; a wrong BMS strangling a healthy pack body diodes; the right BMS protecting a flat pack. Most such boards only release once a charger is applied
Brownouts and the reboot mid-move the BMS choking a full pack the pack actually running down. The original "flat battery" note was right and should not have been struck out
Pack capacity claimed 3S12P — 36 cells, ~30 Ah, ~330 Wh: "it could not drain in an evening" 12 cells, ~9 Ah, ~130 Wh. At the rig's ~18 W that is about seven hours. It drains in an evening comfortably
The lesson worth keeping The number 3S12P was never measured — it was inherited. It sat in the written record, got treated as fact, and carried an entire diagnosis plus a whole revision of the schematic with it. The capacity figure derived from it was even used as the argument that killed the correct explanation. Same failure this project keeps meeting, wearing a document instead of a component: count the cells.

01 What to actually do now

  1. Measure the charger open-circuit, before anything. A 4S Li-ion pack charges to 16.8 V. A 12.6 V supply is a 3S charger and will never fill this pack past about half. 13.8–14.4 V is a lead-acid unit — harmless here at 3.45–3.6 V/cell, but it undercharges. This inverts the earlier warning: on a 3S pack that same charger would have been dangerous; on 4S it is merely inadequate.
  2. Charge the pack. The BMS should release as the charger comes up. If it does not release after a proper 16.8 V charge, then the board is suspect.
  3. Measure the four groups. B−→B1, B1→B2, B2→B3, B3→B+ — each about 4.2 V when full and within 50 mV of the others. The weak group shows up here, and it is the one that tripped the cutoff. Three parallel cells means one tired cell drags a whole group.
  4. Then re-check B− to P−. It should now read a few millivolts. ~0.55 V after a full charge is the board failing; ~0.55 V while flat is the board working.
  5. Check the VLP-16's input range before closing S2. See the warning below — this is the one place going to 4S makes things worse.
New on 4S: S2 hands the lidar up to 16.8 V S2 passes raw pack voltage straight to the VLP-16's interface box. Under the old 3S assumption that leg never exceeded 12.6 V. A fully charged 4S pack is 16.8 V. Check the sensor's own stated input range before that switch is ever closed — if it will not take 16.8 V, that leg needs a regulator. Everything else on the rig is comfortable: the Big Easy Driver takes 8–35 V on M+ (and more volts is more torque), and the 5 V buck takes 4.5–40 V in.
A shorted balance lead on a 3P group is still a fire Three parallel 18650s behind a 24 AWG wire will make that wire glow. If you disturb the taps at all: sleeve them, strain-relieve them where they leave the pack, work one lead at a time, and never let B− touch B+.

02 The wiring rules that still stand

These were right in Rev 3.0 and survive the correction unchanged — they follow from the BMS having its FETs in the negative leg, which is true of the 4S board too.

Every ground lands on P−, never on B− A return wired to B− bypasses the protection FETs, so that load is unprotected — and it keeps draining the pack after the BMS has cut off, straight past the cut-off meant to save the cells. On a pack that has already been run down once, that is exactly the wire that turns a flat pack into a dead one.

The checkable form: exactly one wire in the rig touches B−, and it is the one from the pack. If you can see two, one of them is wrong.
Common port: there is no C− at all The BMS4S now being fitted has no C− pad — charge and discharge share P+ / P−. So the charger's negative goes to the same star point as everything else, and the separate CHG− rail that Rev 3.1 carried is deleted, not moved.

Two things follow, and neither is a wiring choice — they are consequences of the topology. Charge with S1 and S2 open, because the charger now sits in parallel with every load and a CC limit shared with the load never lets the CV stage terminate cleanly. And because the buck is not isolated, the USB-C supply's ground is bonded to the entire rig's ground while charging — use a floating supply, and don't also have the Pi on a mains-earthed brick.
Also settled on the sheet
ItemDecision
U6Deleted. A buck needs ~1.5 V of headroom and never regulated. M+ takes +VSW1 directly — and at 4S it now sees up to 16.8 V, still inside the driver's 8–35 V.
Charge pathUSB-C. PD trigger at 20 V → BCD5A CC/CV buck at 16.8 V / 1.5 A → the fused node, returning to the star point. Charging is fused too. See section 04.
U11INA226, drawn DNP. The pack lead runs straight through it; fitting it means cutting the +VBATT rail between its two drops and letting the shunt bridge the gap. Must be R002 — R100 is good for 0.8 A and this rig pulls ~3 A.
R_PUUnchanged and still the gating item: 10 kΩ from ENABLE to the driver's own VCC, on the driver side of R_EN, so it holds the driver disabled through the Pi's boot and with the Pi unplugged.

04 Charging over USB-C

The parts on hand are a 303PDSink01 PD trigger board (USB-C in, 3-way DIP, screw terminal out) and a BCD5A CC/CV buck. Together with one resistor they make a working 4S charger from a 100 W USB-C supply.

The trigger board is a fixed-voltage source, not a charger Its three DIP switches select from the standard PD ladder — 5 / 9 / 12 / 15 / 20 V. There is no 16.8 V step, which is what a 4S Li-ion pack needs. Three switches also means no PPS: PPS needs a button sequence or I²C, so fine-grained voltage is not available.

20 V straight onto this pack is 5.0 V per cell. That is the setting to be careful of, and on a "100 W" board it is the headline mode. Find the DIP mapping by metering VBUS with nothing connected to the screw terminal, then label the board. You have three of them — dedicate one and mark it.
The chain
StageSet toWhy
USB-C charger100 W20 V × 5 A. Charging at 1.5 A is only ~25 W, so there is five times the headroom needed.
J_USB20 VThe highest fixed step, giving the buck room to regulate.
U1216.8 V20 → 16.8 leaves 3.2 V of headroom. This is the exact failure U6 had — 12 V in, 12 V out, permanently in dropout. This one really does regulate.
U121.5 AThe second pot. About 0.2 C on this ~9 Ah pack — the BMS would allow 20 A, the cells would not thank you. Set it by shorting the output through the meter on its 10 A range.
R_CHGDeletedThe 3.3 Ω resistor existed only because a plain LM2596 has one pot and cannot limit current. The BCD5A has two — that is the whole difference between a supply and a charger — so the dropper is gone.
Five things to get right Set both pots on the meter before it ever sees the pack — and err low on the volts. 16.6 V gives ~95% of capacity; 17.2 V is 4.3 V/cell and damages cells. Then do not touch either pot again.
Charge with S1 and S2 open. Common port puts the charger in parallel with every load; with the rig running, the current limit feeds the load first and the CV taper never terminates cleanly.
Leave it an hour past 16.8 V. The balancer only bleeds near 4.2 V/cell, so that last hour is the entire reason for fitting a balancing board.
The buck is not isolated, so IN− and OUT− are the same copper — drawn on the sheet — and on a common-port board that bonds the USB-C supply's ground to the whole rig's ground. Use a floating supply; do not also have the Pi on a mains-earthed brick.
Do not leave it charging unattended. The BMS cutoff is a backstop, not the control loop, and this pack has already been run flat once.
Worth buying: a hobby balance charger For finding the weak group rather than just refilling the pack, an iMAX B6-class balance charger shows each group's voltage as it charges and balances them. It runs on 11–18 V DC — the same PD trigger at 15 V will power it. It needs a 5-pin JST-XH balance lead tapped off B− and the four taps, which the pack does not currently have.

05 The schematic — one page, every conductor drawn

Nothing on this sheet is joined by name. There are no net labels doing the connecting: the rails are real horizontal wires, the drops are real vertical wires, and every junction dot is a real node. A crossing without a dot is genuinely not a connection — which is what lets unrelated nets cross freely and still leaves the page unambiguous. The ten rail names are a reading aid; delete every one and the netlist is identical.

How it is checked, now that nothing is joined by name The validator builds a net tracer — union-find over wire endpoints and junction dots — and then asserts the engineering rules by following copper: that the star point reaches every ground and does not reach B−; that the BMS symbol has no C− pin and R_CHG is absent; that each pack tap carries exactly one wire; that R_PU reaches the driver's VCC and not the Pi's 3V3; that the DS3231 and INA226 sit on 3V3 and never 5 V; that coil A is not coil B. Then kicad-cli sch erc runs, and then the sheet gets plotted and looked at. All three found different faults — including KiCad's ERC catching a ground pin the wire merely passed over rather than ended on, which is not a connection.

When the board changed, the two C− rules were inverted, not deleted. A removed rule leaves nothing behind; a rule that asserts the absence of the old topology fails loudly if a later session re-adds it from stale notes — which is exactly the failure this project has already met once.
